title: Beyond Guardrails: Why AI Infrastructure Security Is Hard
summary: Learn why least privilege across network, identity, authorization, and configuration controls are key to AI infrastructure security.
body_markdown:
### Summary


AI infrastructure security requires more than LLM guardrails. Least-privilege network, identity, authorization, and configuration controls can protect distributed AI workloads and help reduce breach impact.


*This is the final article in our three-part series on AI security.*


- **Part 1: “**[What No One Tells You about Securing AI Apps: Demystifying AI Guardrails](https://blog.everpuredata.com/perspectives/securing-ai-applications-demystifying-ai-guardrails/) **”** showed how DevSecOps practices and specialized safety models help keep LLM applications secure and aligned.
- **Part 2: “**[Automating Guardrail Security Policy for Better Monitoring and Access Control](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/guardrail-security-policy-is-all-you-need/) **”** examined the policies that fuel guardrails and how LLM-assisted analysis can help create and maintain them.
- **Part 3: “Beyond Guardrails: Why AI Infrastructure Security Is Hard” (** ***You are here!*** **):** This article focuses on the systems that run AI workloads and the controls that keep those systems resilient.


Model-facing controls answer only part of the security question: *How can policy keep pace across the entire AI ecosystem?*


This post looks at the infrastructure beneath the model. An AI application runs in networks; assumes roles; reads secrets; writes logs; and connects to databases, object stores, queues, and model endpoints. A prompt filter cannot constrain an ECS task role with wildcard S3 access or a security group that permits broad workload-to-workload traffic. Those risks require infrastructure policy.


## **Beyond the prompt: Securing the infrastructure behind AI**


[AI applications are distributed systems](https://www.everpuredata.com/knowledge/what-is-ai-infrastructure.html) . A single application may include containers, functions, queues, databases, object stores, model endpoints, secrets, logging services, and[multiple workload identities](https://www.everpuredata.com/knowledge/ai-workloads.html) . Each component adds a network path, identity, permission, or configuration that can expand the application’s blast radius.


Here, least privilege spans four connected areas:


- **Network:** Allow only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports for north-south traffic entering or leaving the application and east-west traffic between workloads
- **Authentication:** Give each workload a specific, verifiable identity and narrowly scoped trust relationship, using managed credentials instead of shared or static secrets
- **Authorization:** Permit that authenticated identity to perform only the required actions on specific cloud resources, APIs, and data rather than granting wildcard access
- **Configuration hardening:** Enforce secure defaults—such as TLS, encryption, audit logging, and segmentation—that reduce exposure and make the other controls harder to bypass


These controls depend on one another. A narrow IAM policy still leaves risk if the workload has broad network reachability. A precise network rule is incomplete if the workload shares credentials or runs with insecure defaults.


To reduce access safely, security teams need a current application boundary, evidence of its real dependencies, and minimum controls across all four areas. They also need to make those changes without breaking production.


## **Why least privilege is challenging**


“Give every workload only the connectivity and permissions it needs” is easy to state. The application boundary and its required access, however, are not stored in one authoritative place.


[Microsoft’s State of Cloud Permissions Risks report](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoft-entra-blog/2023-state-of-cloud-permissions-risks-report-now-published/1061397) found that workload identities outnumber human identities 10 to 1. On average, 80% of workload identities are inactive and use less than 5% of the permissions granted to them. That leaves a large pool of machine access that may no longer be required but can still expand the impact of a compromise.


###### *Figure 1: Least privilege is difficult because teams must reconstruct a changing application, prove which access is active, coordinate four control areas, and prioritize changes without breaking valid workflows.*


**Rank** **Challenge** **Why It Matters**


1 Required access differs from provisioned access Terraform and configuration show what was provisioned; CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and workload logs show what was actually used. Neither view is complete on its own


2 The live application is hard to reconstruct Resources may share an account or VPC without belonging to the same application, while one application can span services and deployments. Architecture, workflows, and ownership also change, so documentation alone cannot show whether a resource or access path is still active


3 Effective identity access is fragmented Roles appear differently across Terraform, ECS, resource policies, and CloudTrail, while federation and role chaining can obscure the originating caller. Effective permissions also emerge from identity and resource policies, boundaries, session policies, service control policies, and explicit denies; no single policy reveals actual access


4 Least privilege spans multiple control layers Narrowing IAM does not remove broad network reachability, and a precise network rule does not fix shared credentials or insecure configuration


5 Recommendations must be prioritized and deployable Security teams receive more findings than they can address at once. They need usage and risk context to distinguish high-impact exposures from lower-priority cleanup, then policy as code they can validate through existing engineering workflows


Excessive permissions become more dangerous when they overlap with other weaknesses. A 2024[Tenable’s Cloud Risk Report](https://www.tenable.com/press-releases/tenable-cloud-risk-report-sounds-the-alarm-on-toxic-cloud-exposures-threatening-global-organizations) found that 38% of organizations had cloud workloads combining public exposure, a critical vulnerability, and excessive privileges—a combination it calls the “toxic cloud trilogy.” Least privilege does not remove the vulnerability, but it can reduce what an attacker can reach or do after exploiting it.


Architecture documents are useful snapshots, not proof of current behavior. Deployments multiply, workflows change, and ownership passes between teams. The people securing an environment may not know whether a resource, permission, or network path still supports an active workflow.


Usage logs fill part of that gap. CloudTrail shows which principal performed an API action against a resource and when. VPC Flow Logs show which endpoints communicated, on which ports, and how frequently. Workload and service logs add application behavior. Correlating these sources helps separate required access from permissions and network paths that are broad, stale, or unused. It also gives security teams evidence for deciding which changes reduce the most risk.


Identity scope also controls blast radius. In Mandiant engagements involving major cloud and SaaS environments during the second half of 2025,[Google Cloud reported](https://cloud.google.com/security/report/resources/cloud-threat-horizons-report-h1-2026) that threat actors exploited identity issues for initial access in 83% of incidents, while data was targeted in 73% of incidents. When an identity is compromised, least privilege determines how far that access can extend.


## **Next: How ASTRA turns telemetry into least privilege**


At Everpure, security and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams use ASTRA (Automated Service Topology and Risk Analysis) to secure our infrastructure. ASTRA combines infrastructure configuration with observed usage to reconstruct application topologies, identify overbroad access, prioritize least-privilege risks, and generate policy-as-code recommendations.


Our upcoming blog series on ASTRA will answer three questions:


- How does ASTRA infer topology for your application?
- How does ASTRA detect configuration-hardening gaps?
- How does ASTRA prioritize least privilege recommendations?


[ARGOS, our AI policy engine](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/guardrail-security-policy-is-all-you-need/) , will be the running example. The series will follow ASTRA from telemetry to application topology and observed flows, then to prioritized risk and least-privilege Terraform code.
